The manuscript presents a well-structured investigation into the role of microRNA-146a in regulating inflammatory responses in human epithelial cells. The experimental design is generally sound, with appropriate use of qPCR and Western blotting to support the central claims. I particularly appreciate the inclusion of both gain- and loss-of-function experiments, which strengthen the validity of the conclusions. However, there are several concerns that need to be addressed before the manuscript can be considered for publication.

The authors claim in the Discussion that microRNA-146a 'directly suppresses IRAK1 expression,' but this conclusion is not fully supported by the data. While the luciferase assay in Figure 4C suggests binding, it lacks mutation controls for the seed sequence, which are necessary to confirm target specificity. This limitation should be acknowledged, and the claim should be tempered.

Additionally, the sample size for the in vitro experiments (n=3 biological replicates) is minimal, and no power analysis is provided. The authors should justify this choice or clarify whether preliminary data support sufficient effect sizes.

The introduction provides adequate background, though it could more clearly differentiate this work from previously published studies on miR-146a in immune cells. A brief comparison to findings in macrophages (e.g., Taganov et al., 2006) would help position the novelty of the current study.

Overall, the work is promising and technically competent, but requires moderate revisions to strengthen the mechanistic claims and contextualize the findings. I recommend major revision.

state: Reviewer 2: I have completed my evaluation of the manuscript titled 'Investigative Analysis of Cell Membrane Permeability Under Variable Electromagnetic Frequencies' (Manuscript ID: JBCR-2024-8876). The submission was received via the online editorial system on April 3, 2024, and assigned to me on April 5, following the standard triage procedure based on declared expertise in biophysics and cellular electrophysiology. I confirm that I have no conflicts of interest with any of the authors, nor have I collaborated with them in the past five years. The journal’s guidelines for reviewers were consulted during the preparation of this report, particularly sections 3.1 (Evaluation Criteria) and 4.2 (Ethical Considerations). The review was conducted over a period of nine working days, primarily between April 6 and April 15, during which time I accessed the manuscript document (version 1.0, PDF format) and supplementary data files (Data_S1.xlsx and Video_S1.mp4) on three separate occasions. My initial read-through occurred on April 6, followed by a detailed assessment of the methodology and results on April 10, and a final synthesis of comments on April 14. I used a desktop computer running Windows 11 with Adobe Acrobat Pro DC for document annotation and cross-referencing. I did not share the manuscript or any part of it with colleagues or assistants, nor did I upload it to any cloud-based collaboration platform. All notes were kept in a password-protected local folder labeled 'JBCR_Review_8876'. The manuscript comprises 28 pages, including 5 figures and 3 tables, and is structured into the standard IMRaD format. The abstract provides a general overview of the experimental setup but lacks specificity regarding exposure parameters. The introduction spans 6.5 pages and cites 87 references, predominantly from the past decade, though several foundational papers from the 1990s appear to be missing. The methods section describes the cell culture conditions, electromagnetic exposure apparatus, and permeability assays, but certain details—such as the exact waveform modulation type and calibration frequency of the signal generator—are omitted. The results are presented clearly in graphical form, though statistical reporting is inconsistent across figures; for instance, Figure 3 includes p-values for all comparisons, whereas Figure 4 reports only trends without significance testing. The discussion interprets the observed permeability changes in relation to prior in vitro studies but does not address potential thermal confounders. Several minor typographical errors were noted (e.g., 'recieved' on page 12, line 8), but these do not impede comprehension. The supplementary video shows a representative assay run, though the time-lapse resolution is insufficient to assess transient effects. The authors have made the raw data available, which I reviewed briefly, but no data validation scripts were included. I recommend that the authors consider shortening the introduction by consolidating overlapping paragraphs and expanding the methods to include equipment model numbers and software versions. Additionally, a power analysis should be added to justify sample sizes. No ethical concerns were identified regarding the use of human or animal cells. The research question is moderately relevant to the journal’s scope, though similar findings have been reported in peripheral models. While the experimental design appears generally sound, the absence of blinding during image analysis raises concerns about potential observer bias. The conclusions are somewhat overstated given the preliminary nature of the in vivo extrapolations. I have no concerns about plagiarism or data fabrication based on initial similarity checks. The reference list follows the journal’s style with only minor deviations. I intend to complete my second pending review for this journal by April 20. I have served as a reviewer for this journal for seven years and have handled 23 manuscripts to date. The manuscript was delivered within the requested timeframe, despite a brief extension granted due to institutional server outages during the second week of April. I did not consult any external sources beyond the manuscript and its supplements. The overall presentation falls short of the journal’s usual standards for clarity and rigor. The authors should revise the manuscript to improve technical transparency and analytical completeness.

I recommend rejection unless the authors can provide stronger statistical support, address the overinterpretation of preliminary findings, and remove references to non-public research. With these changes, the paper could be reconsidered. My confidence in this recommendation is high, given my expertise in neurodegenerative mechanisms and direct experience with the models used.

Reviewer #3:

The manuscript presents an interesting application of machine learning to predict protein folding patterns in thermophilic organisms. The methodology appears generally sound, with appropriate use of cross-validation and a reasonably diverse training dataset. The results show a modest improvement over existing models, which could be meaningful in niche applications. However, I am uncertain whether this work represents a sufficient advance over current methods to warrant publication in this journal.

On one hand, the model’s performance gain—while statistically significant—is small in practical terms, and the authors do not thoroughly discuss limitations in generalizability to mesophilic or extremophilic species outside the training set. The experimental design does not include ablation studies to justify architectural choices, which weakens the interpretability of the results.

On the other hand, the data preprocessing pipeline is well-documented, and the code is publicly available with clear documentation, which enhances reproducibility. The authors also compare their approach to three established baselines, which strengthens the validity of their claims.

That said, my primary concern is that my expertise lies more in ecological bioinformatics than structural biology or deep learning architectures. While I can evaluate the general scientific rigor, I may not be best positioned to assess the technical novelty of the neural network design. Similarly, the paper’s focus on algorithmic performance edges into computational biophysics, which is somewhat outside my core domain.

Given these uncertainties, I cannot confidently recommend acceptance or rejection. The work is competently executed but may be more appropriate for a specialized computational biology venue. Further input from a reviewer with deeper expertise in protein structure prediction models would be valuable.

This manuscript does not cite that work, nor does it address the thermodynamic barriers highlighted in my research.

The methods section is vague, with no clear description of how quantum states are simulated or measured. The results appear speculative, and the discussion overreaches without supporting evidence. Given the fundamental issues with the theoretical framework—issues I have extensively documented—the paper, in its current form, cannot be considered for publication. A major conceptual revision would be necessary, but even then, the core premise remains highly questionable.

I am confident in this assessment, given my direct involvement in related research. The topic is of interest, but this submission does not meet the scientific standards required for publication in this journal.

state: Reviewer #3: I have now completed my evaluation of the manuscript entitled "Investigating the Role of Microplastic Accumulation in Intertidal Sediments Along the Eastern Seaboard," submitted to *Marine Environmental Research Communications*. The work presents data collected from 18 sampling sites between Maine and Virginia over a 14-month period from March 2022 to May 2023. I appreciate the effort put into field sampling, particularly the use of quadrat-based collection methods and the inclusion of grain size analysis to contextualize sediment composition. The authors have organized the manuscript into standard sections: abstract, introduction, methods, results, discussion, and references. The abstract clearly states the objective, though I noted a typo in the second sentence—"micro-plastics" appears with a hyphen inconsistently throughout the document, which should be standardized per journal style. The introduction spans four paragraphs and cites 12 references, which is adequate though slightly light given the scope; additional citations from recent reviews on polymer degradation in marine environments (e.g., Thompson et al. 2021, *Environmental Science & Technology*) would strengthen the background. In the methods section, subsection 2.3 describes sieve mesh sizes used for particle separation—300 μm and 500 μm—but does not clarify whether samples were pre-treated with hydrogen peroxide to remove organic matter, a standard protocol in such studies. This omission raises concerns about potential organic contamination affecting particle counts. The statistical analysis described in 2.5 employs one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s post hoc test to compare regional differences; this is appropriate, but the software used (stated as "a commercial package") should be named—was it SPSS v28, R v4.2.1, or another? The results are presented in three figures and two tables. Figure 1, a map of sampling locations, is clear but lacks a scale bar, which is a basic cartographic requirement. Table 1 reports mean microplastic concentrations per kg of dry sediment; the values range from 18.4 to 217.6, which appears plausible. However, the confidence intervals in Table 1 are listed as standard deviations—this should be clarified, as the text refers to them as 95% CIs but the values match SDs. The discussion interprets the north-to-south gradient in particle load as correlated with population density, which is reasonable, but does not sufficiently consider riverine input or coastal current patterns, both of which are known to influence distribution. Paragraph 4 of the discussion cites a 2020 study from the Baltic Sea as a parallel case, but that system has markedly different hydrodynamics, so the comparison may be overextended. Several minor grammatical issues appear—for instance, on page 9, line 12, "their" is used where "there" is intended. Additionally, reference #7 is cited in-text but missing from the reference list, which needs correction. The conclusion reiterates main findings but does not explicitly suggest policy implications or future monitoring directions, which would enhance impact. Overall, the study is methodologically sound and addresses an important environmental issue, though improvements in clarity, completeness, and contextualization are needed. I have discussed the manuscript in detail with two colleagues during a departmental journal club meeting last Thursday, and we agreed on several points regarding analytical rigor. One colleague suggested that the polymer identification via FTIR could benefit from reporting the minimum spectrum quality threshold, which I now recommend the authors include. Given the collective input, I believe the manuscript can be improved to meet publication standards. I recommend major revisions, and I am confident in this assessment.

Recommendation: Revise
Confidence: Moderate

The manuscript titled "An Investigation into Cell Proliferation Dynamics Under Variable Oxygen Conditions" presents a topic of general interest within the field of cellular biology, particularly in relation to hypoxic environments and their influence on metabolic activity. The subject matter aligns broadly with ongoing research in cancer metabolism and tissue engineering, both of which are active areas in current biomedical science. The authors have structured the paper in a conventional manner, beginning with an introduction that outlines the importance of oxygen tension in cell culture, followed by methods, results, and discussion sections. The formatting adheres to the journal’s guidelines, with numbered pages, line spacing consistent with the template, and figures placed appropriately within the text.

I noted that the reference list includes a mix of recent publications and foundational papers, with citations spanning the last two decades. The language throughout is largely comprehensible, though there are occasional grammatical constructions that could be clarified, such as passive voice usage in the methods section. For example, on page 5, the phrase "it was observed that cells exhibited changes" could be revised to "we observed changes in cell behavior" for improved clarity and directness. The abstract summarizes the experimental conditions and outcomes in a standard fashion, though it does not clearly differentiate the novelty of the findings from prior studies.

The figures are legible and labeled, with axis titles present and units indicated. Figure 2, in particular, shows a time-series plot with error bars, which is appropriate for the data type. However, the resolution of Figure 3 appears slightly pixelated in the submitted version, which may affect readability in print. The supplementary materials include raw data tables, which is commendable for transparency, though they are not referenced directly in the main text, making their relevance unclear.

The methods section describes the cell lines used, the incubation conditions, and the assay protocols. It mentions the use of spectrophotometry to measure proliferation, which is a standard technique. However, the description does not specify the exact wavelength used for absorbance measurements, nor does it detail the calibration process for the instrument. These omissions may affect reproducibility, though similar gaps are common in manuscripts at this stage.

In the discussion, the authors suggest that low oxygen levels correlate with increased proliferation rates, which they interpret as a potential adaptive mechanism. This interpretation is plausible within the existing literature, though the conclusion is somewhat broad given the limited number of cell types examined. The authors do acknowledge this limitation in the final paragraph, which strengthens the overall honesty of the report.

One general concern is the lack of statistical analysis details. While the text mentions "significant differences" in growth rates, the specific tests used (e.g., t-test, ANOVA) are not named, and p-values are reported without correction for multiple comparisons. This weakens the interpretability of the results. Additionally, the sample size for each condition is stated as n=3, which is typical but not justified with a power analysis.

Overall, the study follows a logical sequence and addresses a relevant question. The writing could benefit from editing for precision, and the methods would be more robust with additional technical detail. The conclusions are generally supported by the data presented, though some claims extend beyond what the evidence directly shows.

The central finding—that reduced oxygen increases proliferation in this system—is not convincingly demonstrated because the primary dataset contains unexplained outliers in the control group that were not addressed in the analysis, and no justification is provided for their exclusion.

Reviewer #2

The manuscript presents an analysis of cellulose nanofiber extraction from agricultural waste using enzymatic pretreatment, followed by mechanical fibrillation. While the topic is relevant to sustainable materials research, the experimental design raises concerns. The authors claim a 40% increase in yield compared to acid hydrolysis methods (page 8, Table 2), but the enzymatic process was only tested at a single enzyme loading (20 FPU/g), with no dose-response data to support optimization. Without comparison across multiple loadings, the claim of efficiency is premature. Additionally, the characterization in Figure 4 shows wide standard deviations in fiber diameter measurements (ranging from 15 to 60 nm), yet the text describes the product as 'uniform'—this overstatement is not supported by the data. The discussion section (pp. 11–13) fails to address prior work by Zhang et al. (2021) on similar substrates, which reported comparable yields under milder conditions. This omission weakens the novelty argument. On a positive note, the environmental impact assessment in Section 3.5 is thorough and well-documented, providing clear life-cycle metrics that strengthen the paper’s broader relevance. The writing is generally clear, though some technical terms (e.g., 'high-intensity dispersion') lack methodological detail, making replication difficult. I recommend additional experiments to validate the yield claims and a revised discussion that contextualizes the findings within existing literature. Clarification of the dispersion parameters and improved statistical reporting would also enhance rigor. At present, the conclusions are not sufficiently substantiated for publication.

The manuscript presents an interesting hypothesis regarding neural plasticity in adult learners, supported by a behavioral experiment involving language acquisition tasks. The general approach is sound, but several issues need to be addressed before the work can be considered for publication.

The introduction frames the research question adequately, though it omits recent findings from fMRI studies in similar paradigms (e.g., Smith et al. 2023; Lee & Kumar, 2022), which should be integrated to better position the novelty of the current work. More critically, the methods section lacks sufficient detail about the participant selection criteria—specifically, how bilingual proficiency was quantified. Without this, replication is impossible.

Additionally, the discussion overreaches by implying clinical applications in language rehabilitation, despite no data involving patient populations. This claim should be tempered or reframed as speculative.

That said, I am unable to select any of the standard recommendation options provided in the review portal because none accurately reflect the nuanced outcome I suggest—specifically, a conditional revision pending methodological clarification and contextual refinement of the conclusions. A new option for such cases would be helpful.

The discussion section would benefit from a more balanced interpretation of the limitations, particularly regarding long-term stability of the dispersions, which was not assessed. Including at least a brief discussion of potential degradation mechanisms would improve the paper’s impact.

The writing is clear and figures are well-prepared, though minor grammatical edits are needed. I recommend the authors expand the methodology to include sonication amplitude calibration details and provide raw data for particle size distribution in the supplement.

I will complete my assessment after considering the authors’ responses to these points.

The experimental design is generally sound, with appropriate controls and a sufficient sample size. However, I have significant concerns about the statistical methods used in the analysis of the electrophysiological data. I also note that the literature review omits several key studies from the past five years, particularly work by Zhang et al. Reviewer Number: 3
Recommendation: Revise
Confidence Rating: Moderate

The manuscript titled 'An Exploration of Cellulose-Based Nanocomposites for Enhanced Water Filtration in Semi-Arid Agricultural Zones' presents a topic of considerable relevance given the increasing global focus on sustainable water purification technologies. The general structure of the document follows a conventional scientific format, beginning with an abstract that outlines the purpose, methodology, and anticipated outcomes. The introduction provides a broad overview of water scarcity issues, particularly in semi-arid regions, and discusses the role of filtration membranes in mitigating contamination risks. It references several key studies from the past decade, including works published in Environmental Science & Technology and the Journal of Membrane Science, though the citations appear to be somewhat dated, with only two references from the past three years. The literature review attempts to position the current study within existing research, but it lacks a critical synthesis of competing methodologies or comparative performance metrics.

The methods section describes a multi-step fabrication process involving the dissolution of microcrystalline cellulose in an ionic liquid, followed by ultrasonication and phase inversion to produce asymmetric membranes. The authors indicate that three different nanofiller concentrations (0.5%, 1.0%, and 1.5% w/w) were tested, with each formulation cast using a doctor blade at a fixed gap of 200 µm. Characterization was performed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), and tensile strength analysis. Filtration efficiency was assessed using synthetic wastewater spiked with E. coli and turbidity agents. The reported flow rates and log-reduction values are presented in Table 2, though the table lacks error bars or standard deviation indicators, making it difficult to assess reproducibility. The discussion section reiterates the results without offering a deeper interpretation of why the 1.0% filler sample outperformed others, nor does it adequately address potential limitations such as membrane fouling over extended operation or scalability of the ionic liquid recovery process.

Several figures are included: Figure 1 shows the schematic of the fabrication setup, which appears to be adapted from a previously published protocol with minimal modifications. Figure 2 presents SEM micrographs of the membrane cross-sections, but the images are low resolution and lack scale bars, undermining their diagnostic value. Figure 3 plots flux decline over a 6-hour period, but the axis labels are inconsistent—time is labeled in both minutes and hours across subpanels, which may be a typographical error. The conclusion section rephrases the abstract and does not introduce new insights or suggest concrete applications.

Minor grammatical issues are present throughout, such as inconsistent use of past and present tense in the results section, and several instances of redundant phrasing (e.g., 'very unique', 'completely full'). The reference list contains 38 entries, formatted in a manner that approximates APA style but with irregularities in journal title capitalization and missing DOIs for several articles. There is no mention of ethical approval or data availability, though the study does not appear to involve human subjects or proprietary datasets.

While the topic is relevant and the experimental approach is generally sound, the manuscript in its current form does not sufficiently differentiate itself from prior work or justify the novelty claim implied in the title. The data presentation requires substantial improvement to meet the journal’s standards.

The manuscript fails to disclose that the lead author is a former graduate student of Reviewer Number 3, with whom they have co-authored two prior papers, creating a significant conflict of interest that was not declared in the submission system.

The manuscript presents a novel approach to modeling forest carbon sequestration using remote sensing data, which is timely and potentially impactful. The introduction clearly outlines the research gap, and the objectives are well defined. However, several critical issues require attention before publication.

The methodology section (Section 2.3) describes a machine learning model trained on MODIS data, but the choice of hyperparameters is not justified. The authors state they used "default settings" without referencing why these are appropriate or how sensitivity analyses were conducted. This undermines reproducibility. I recommend including a supplementary table detailing hyperparameter selection and cross-validation results.

Figure 4 claims a 15% improvement in prediction accuracy over existing models, but no statistical test is reported to support this. The authors should perform a paired t-test or similar and report p-values. Additionally, the uncertainty intervals in Figure 5 are unusually narrow—please clarify whether bootstrapping or another method was used and confirm sample size adequacy.

The discussion appropriately contextualizes findings within recent literature, citing Smith et al. 2022 and Lee & Gupta 2023. However, the claim that this method "will transform forest monitoring practices" (p. 12) is overstated given the regional scope of validation. Please moderate language and acknowledge limitations in scalability.

One overlooked issue is the lack of ground-truth data from tropical forests, which limits generalizability. This should be explicitly addressed in the limitations paragraph.

Overall, the paper is promising but requires targeted revisions to strengthen methodological transparency and interpretative rigor. With these changes, it would be suitable for publication.

Manuscript ID: IJTE-2026-0482
Title: An Exploratory Analysis of Cellulose-Based Paper Substrates in Low-Temperature Printing Applications
Date of Review: March 10, 2026
Confidence: High
Recommendation: Minor Revision

This review is submitted in accordance with the peer review guidelines established by the International Journal of Technology in Education (IJTE), adhering to the structured format as outlined in the reviewer portal. The manuscript has been evaluated for alignment with the journal’s scope, which includes interdisciplinary research at the intersection of material science and applied educational technologies. The submission was received via the online editorial system, and all sections appear to be present: Abstract, Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion, and References. The document follows the required 12-point Times New Roman font, 1-inch margins, and double-spacing as specified in the IJTE template. No obvious formatting deviations were observed, including proper labeling of figures and tables, though Table 2 appears to have a minor alignment issue in the third column that does not impede readability.

The abstract provides a general overview of the study’s intent, namely to assess the performance of three cellulose-based paper substrates under low-temperature thermal printing conditions. The research question is framed within the context of sustainable printing solutions, which is a relevant and growing area of interest in both industrial applications and academic research. The introduction situates the work among existing literature on biodegradable substrates, citing key sources from the past decade, including works by Zhang et al. (2021), Müller and Tran (2019), and a foundational paper by O’Donnell (2017) on fiber matrix stability. While these references are appropriate, the introduction could benefit from a more precise articulation of the knowledge gap this study aims to fill. At present, the rationale for selecting the specific temperature range (55–65°C) is implied but not explicitly justified.

The Methods section describes the sample preparation protocol in adequate detail, specifying the source of the paper substrates (commercially available notebook sheets from three regional suppliers), the printer model used (HP ThermalJet 4200), and the calibration procedures for temperature control. The experimental design includes three replicates per substrate type, which is acceptable for preliminary testing. However, the statistical analysis is limited to mean and standard deviation, without inferential tests such as ANOVA, which would strengthen the validity of the comparisons. This is not a critical flaw but should be addressed in revision.

The Results section presents data on print clarity, ink absorption rate, and surface degradation, with supporting figures (Figures 1–3). The figures are clearly labeled and consistent with the text. The Discussion interprets the findings in relation to substrate porosity and lignin content, drawing reasonable conclusions. There is a brief mention of potential applications in classroom settings, which aligns with the journal’s educational focus, though this connection remains underdeveloped.

One minor concern is the reference list, which includes six sources published by the same small open-access publisher, all within the past three years. While this does not necessarily indicate an issue, it warrants attention to ensure citation balance. Language and grammar are generally sound, with only a few typographical errors (e.g., 'temparature' on page 5).

In sum, the manuscript contributes modestly to the field of sustainable printing materials and is generally well-structured. The work is not groundbreaking, but it is methodologically sound and suitable for the journal’s audience. The requested revisions are minor and primarily editorial. I recommend publication pending clarification of the temperature selection rationale and inclusion of a basic statistical comparison.

The experimental data, as presented, were generated using equipment previously described in a 2023 conference proceeding authored by the second reviewer of this manuscript, whose affiliation overlaps with one of the authors’ institutions, and this relationship has not been disclosed.

The manuscript titled 'An Investigation into the Effects of Compound X on Cellular Proliferation in Cultured Human Fibroblasts' presents a topic of potential interest to the field of cellular biology, particularly in the context of regenerative medicine and pharmacological intervention strategies. The general structure of the paper follows the conventional IMRaD format, which is appreciated. The abstract provides a summary of the objectives, methods, results, and conclusions, though it leans slightly toward being descriptive rather than interpretive. The introduction begins with a broad overview of cell proliferation mechanisms, which is standard, and gradually narrows to the specific compound under study. There is a citation of several foundational papers in the area of growth factor signaling, including works from the early 2010s, which helps situate the current study within the existing literature. However, the transition from general mechanisms to the specific rationale for selecting Compound X could be more clearly articulated. The methods section details the cell culture conditions, passage numbers, media composition, and dosing concentrations. The use of DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS is standard, and the incubation conditions (37°C, 5% CO2) are correctly reported. The description of the MTT assay protocol is adequate, though the version of the assay kit used (if any) is not specified, which may affect reproducibility. The statistical analysis mentions the use of one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s post-hoc test, which is appropriate for the experimental design involving multiple treatment groups. The results are presented in three figures: one showing dose-dependent effects, another time-course data, and a third demonstrating protein expression levels via Western blot. The figure legends are sufficiently detailed, though Figure 2 could benefit from clearer labeling of the time points. The Western blot in Figure 3 includes bands for phosphorylated ERK and total ERK, which supports the proposed mechanism of action, but the loading controls appear slightly uneven, which raises a minor concern about normalization. The discussion reiterates the main findings and attempts to link them to prior studies on kinase activation pathways. There is an acknowledgment of the study’s limitations, such as the use of a single cell type and the absence of in vivo validation. The conclusion aligns with the data presented and avoids overstatement. References are formatted consistently and include a mix of primary research articles and review papers, with a reasonable balance of recent and classic citations. The writing is generally clear, though there are several instances of awkward phrasing, such as on page 5 where the sentence structure disrupts the logical flow. There are also minor typographical errors, including a missing space after a comma in Table 1. The supplementary materials include raw absorbance values and gel images, which is commendable for transparency. Overall, the study appears to have been conducted with appropriate controls and sufficient technical rigor. That said, the central claim regarding the novel mechanism of Compound X is not sufficiently supported by the data, as the key experiment demonstrating direct binding to the proposed receptor target was not performed.

Manus. ID: JNE-2024-8871
Manuscript Title: Investigating the Role of Microfibril Alignment in Early-Stage Cellulose Gelation
Date of Review: 2024-05-17
Recommendation: Major Revision
Confidence: High

The manuscript presents a topic within a domain I have engaged with extensively over the past 15 years, particularly regarding biopolymer structuring and hydrodynamic modeling in gel-phase transitions. The general subject area is well aligned with my ongoing research activities, including work currently under review at another journal focusing on fibrillar kinetics in polysaccharide networks. I note that the authors have followed the formatting guidelines of the journal, using 11-point Times New Roman, double spacing, and including line numbers, which facilitates readability. The abstract is structured appropriately, with clear sections for background, methods, results, and conclusion. However, the terminology used in the introduction occasionally diverges from standard nomenclature—specifically, the use of 'microfibril lattice condensation' instead of the more widely accepted 'anisotropic coalescence phase'—though this may simply reflect evolving usage in the subfield.

Section 2.1 describes the ultrasonication protocol in sufficient detail, though I wonder whether the pulse duration (3 seconds on, 2 seconds off) was optimized across multiple pilot runs. The authors cite Smith et al. 2021 for their dispersion method, which is appropriate, though I published a critique of that protocol in Langmuir in 2022 highlighting reproducibility issues under high ionic strength conditions, a scenario relevant here due to the sodium chloride concentration used. The rheological data in Figure 3 appears consistent with expected viscoelastic behavior, though the error bars are quite large in the 0.1–1 Hz range, suggesting potential instability in sample homogeneity. It would be helpful if the authors included a supplementary video of the shear alignment process, as static images in Figure 4 do not fully convey dynamic reorientation.

I have minor concerns about the statistical treatment in Table 2. The use of ANOVA without post-hoc testing for multi-group comparisons is acceptable only if the overall F-test is significant, which is not explicitly stated. Additionally, the sample size (n=4 per condition) is at the lower limit for parametric analysis, and non-parametric alternatives like Kruskal-Wallis might have been more robust. The discussion section reiterates the results without sufficient integration with prior literature—particularly missing is any reference to the 2023 study by Tanaka et al. on cellulose phase separation, which reported conflicting temperature dependence. While not directly overlapping, that work raises questions about the universality of the nucleation threshold proposed here.

I shared a draft of this review with a colleague in my research group who is preparing a related manuscript on cellulose self-assembly, as we were discussing methodological parallels. They suggested that the XRD peak assignments in Section 3.2 might benefit from deconvolution analysis, which I agree with, though I did not include this in my comments since it was not my original observation. The reference list is comprehensive, though it omits several recent preprints from the Nordic Biomaterials Consortium that are directly relevant. In terms of broader impact, the work contributes incrementally to the field but does not introduce a novel mechanism or transformative technique. The conclusions are generally supported by the data, though overstated in the claim of 'predictive reliability' for industrial applications.

The paper requires major revisions, particularly in framing, statistical validation, and contextualization within recent advances. I recommend rejection unless the authors can provide additional experimental validation of their kinetic model, ideally through time-resolved SAXS measurements. Given the overlap with my own pending submission, I believe my assessment remains objective, but I acknowledge the connection for transparency.

Manuscript ID: JNEUROSCI-2024-123456R1
Title: Neural Correlates of Auditory Processing in Mild Cognitive Impairment: A Longitudinal fMRI Study
Date of Review: April 5, 2025

I have now had the opportunity to review the revised version of the above-referenced manuscript, which was resubmitted following the initial round of peer review. The authors have responded to prior comments and made several modifications to the text, including updates to the Methods section, clarification of statistical procedures, and minor rephrasing in the Discussion. The manuscript is formatted in accordance with the journal’s current guidelines, including appropriate section headings, double-spacing, and correctly labeled figure captions. The abstract remains structured with Background, Methods, Results, and Conclusion, and the word count falls within the acceptable range for the journal’s article type. References are cited using the Vancouver style, and all DOIs are present and functional upon spot-checking.

The Introduction begins with a general overview of cognitive decline in aging populations, citing several recent epidemiological studies from the past five years. It transitions into a discussion of auditory processing deficits as potential early markers of neurodegenerative change, referencing foundational work in the field, including seminal papers by Griffith (2017) and Lee et al. (2019). The authors state their hypothesis clearly in the final paragraph: that individuals with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) will exhibit reduced activation in the primary auditory cortex during a phoneme discrimination task, and that this reduction will correlate with performance on delayed recall measures over a 12-month period. This hypothesis is logically derived from the background presented, though the rationale for selecting a 12-month interval over shorter or longer follow-up periods is not elaborated.

The Methods section describes a cohort of 42 participants (21 diagnosed with MCI, 21 age-matched controls) recruited from a university-affiliated memory clinic. Inclusion criteria are clearly defined, including MMSE scores between 24 and 27 for the MCI group and above 27 for controls, absence of major neurological conditions, and normal hearing as confirmed by audiometry. The fMRI protocol is detailed, including scanner type (3T Siemens Prisma), sequence parameters (TR = 2000 ms, TE = 30 ms, voxel size 3 mm³), and task design (block-based with alternating active and rest conditions). Preprocessing steps are listed: slice-timing correction, motion correction, spatial smoothing with a 6 mm FWHM kernel, and normalization to MNI space. Statistical analysis was conducted using SPM12 with a whole-brain FWE-corrected threshold of p < 0.05. The supplementary materials include a table of motion parameters, which shows average framewise displacement below 0.2 mm in all participants, suggesting minimal motion artifact.

The Results section reports significantly reduced BOLD response in the left Heschl’s gyrus (peak MNI: -42, -20, 8; t = 4.62) during the phoneme task in the MCI group compared to controls. Additional clusters are noted in the planum temporale and superior temporal gyrus. Correlation analysis shows a moderate positive relationship (r = 0.41, p = 0.03) between auditory cortex activation and delayed recall scores at follow-up. These findings are illustrated in Figure 2, which displays statistical maps overlaid on a standard brain template, and Figure 3, which presents scatterplots of activation versus cognitive scores.

The Discussion reiterates the main findings and suggests their potential relevance for early detection strategies. The authors acknowledge limitations, including the modest sample size and the lack of pathological confirmation of neurodegenerative status. They also note that auditory tasks were not controlled for semantic content, which may have introduced confounding variables. No new data are introduced in this section, and the conclusions are generally consistent with the results.

While the study is methodologically sound and the data appear robust, the manuscript does not substantially advance the field beyond existing literature. The findings are consistent with prior reports of sensory processing deficits in MCI, and the longitudinal component does not reveal novel trajectories or predictive utility beyond what has already been published. The analytical approach is appropriate, and the data are presented transparently. However, the incremental contribution to scientific knowledge is limited. The authors have adequately addressed prior reviewer concerns. Recommendation: reject. Confidence: high.

I have now had the opportunity to read through the manuscript entitled "Dynamic Interactions Between Soil Microbiota and Root Exudates in Temperate Agroecosystems" (Manuscript ID: JSPB-2024-88765) in full, including all supplementary materials provided. The paper is submitted to the Journal of Soil and Plant Biology, and falls within my general area of expertise, though I should note that my primary research focus over the past five years has been on rhizosphere nutrient cycling in boreal systems, which are somewhat distinct from the temperate systems addressed here. That said, I have taught graduate-level courses in soil microbiology and have served as an external examiner for several PhD theses related to microbial community dynamics, so I believe I am reasonably well-positioned to assess the methodological rigor and conceptual framing of this work.

The authors present a multi-season field study combining metagenomic sequencing with root exudate profiling across three agricultural sites in the Midwest. Their central claim is that certain keystone bacterial taxa exhibit consistent responsiveness to specific classes of exudates, particularly flavonoids and organic acids, and that these interactions are modulated by soil pH and moisture content. The experimental design appears sound at first glance, with appropriate replication (n=4 plots per site) and sampling intervals aligned with key phenological stages. The use of both 16S rRNA sequencing and shotgun metagenomics adds depth, and the statistical models account for several relevant covariates.

That being said, there are several aspects of the methodology that warrant clarification. The section on DNA extraction (page 12) mentions the use of a commercial kit but does not specify the lot number or any modifications to the manufacturer’s protocol, which could affect yield and bias. Additionally, the bioinformatics pipeline, while referencing QIIME2 and MetaPhlAn4, lacks sufficient detail in the supplementary methods to allow for full reproducibility—specifically, the filtering thresholds for low-abundance ASVs and the criteria for functional annotation are not clearly defined. The authors also appear to have pooled samples across sites for certain analyses without testing for site-specific effects first, which risks masking important spatial heterogeneity.

On the presentation side, Figures 3 and 4 are somewhat overcrowded, and the color scheme in Figure 5 may not be accessible to readers with color vision deficiencies. I recommend the use of distinct line patterns or symbols in addition to color. The discussion section is thorough and appropriately cautious in its interpretations, though it could more explicitly acknowledge the limitations of inferring functional activity from taxonomic and gene presence data alone.

I shared a draft of this review with Dr. Lillian Cho, a colleague in the Department of Environmental Microbiology at Central Plains University, primarily to confirm my understanding of the statistical model used in Table 2. She suggested that the authors might consider including a random effect for site in their mixed-effects models, which I now echo as a recommendation. Dr. Cho has no direct connection to this manuscript, but she did co-author a review article with two of the present authors in 2022 on related topics in rhizosphere ecology.

In preparing this review, I also consulted a preprint posted last month by a research group at Northern Ridge Institute, which reports similar findings in a comparable agroecosystem. While that work has not yet undergone peer review, it raises questions about the novelty of the current findings, particularly regarding the role of Pseudomonas spp. in flavonoid degradation. I have attached a copy of my correspondence with a postdoc from that group for the editor’s reference.

Overall, the study addresses a relevant question with a generally appropriate approach. With moderate revisions to clarify methods, improve figure accessibility, and refine the statistical analysis, this manuscript could make a valuable contribution to the literature. I recommend revision, but not rejection, at this stage.

The manuscript should not be accepted because one of the authors is my former graduate student, and we are currently co-developing a grant proposal on a closely related topic, which creates a significant conflict of interest that I failed to disclose at the outset of this review.

Manuscript ID: JNEURO-2025-88912
Title: Neural Correlates of Decision-Making Under Ambiguity: An fMRI Study in Young Adults
Date of Review: March 4, 2026

I have reviewed the manuscript titled 'Neural Correlates of Decision-Making Under Ambiguity: An fMRI Study in Young Adults' submitted to the Journal of Neurocognitive Research. The formatting appears generally compliant with the journal’s current template, though I did notice that the line spacing in the reference section on pages 14–15 seems slightly more compressed than required—possibly due to a formatting glitch in the Word-to-PDF conversion. This is a minor issue but worth noting for production purposes. The abstract follows the conventional structure: background, objectives, methods, results, and conclusion. However, the use of the phrase 'significant brain activation' in the abstract is vague and could be misinterpreted; it would be better to specify regions and statistical thresholds.

The introduction begins with a broad overview of decision-making literature, citing foundational works by Kahneman and Tversky (1979) and more recent studies by Hsu et al. (2015) and Smith & Lee (2020). The progression from general concepts to the specific research question is logical, though the transition between paragraph 3 and 4 feels abrupt. There is a citation missing after the sentence on risk aversion in adolescent populations—possibly an oversight during revisions. The authors state their hypothesis clearly in the final paragraph, which is commendable.

The methods section describes a sample of 42 participants, aged 18–24, recruited from a university subject pool. The inclusion and exclusion criteria are listed, though the criterion regarding 'no history of neurological disorders' relies solely on self-report, which is a limitation worth mentioning. The experimental task is a modified version of the Balloon Analogue Risk Task (BART), adapted for ambiguity conditions. The fMRI acquisition parameters are standard: 3T scanner, gradient-echo EPI sequence, TR = 2000 ms, TE = 30 ms, 32 axial slices, voxel size 3×3×3 mm. Preprocessing steps are adequately described—slice timing correction, realignment, normalization to MNI space, and smoothing with an 8mm kernel. The use of FSL’s FEAT for first-level analysis is appropriate. The second-level analysis employed a mixed-effects model, which is suitable for the design.

In the results section, the authors report activation in the anterior insula and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex during high-ambiguity trials. The statistical threshold is set at p < 0.001 uncorrected, with cluster-level FWE correction at p < 0.05. While the findings are presented clearly, the lack of correction for multiple comparisons at the voxel level raises concerns about false positives. The figures (particularly Figure 2) are of high resolution, though the color scale in panel B appears inconsistent with the legend.

The discussion interprets the findings in the context of salience network involvement, which is reasonable. However, the authors overstate the novelty of their results by claiming 'first evidence of insular modulation under non-risk-based uncertainty,' which is not supported—similar findings were reported by Kim et al. (2022) in a nearly identical paradigm. This should be revised to avoid overstatement.

The supplementary materials include raw behavioral data and a list of excluded participants, which is helpful. The data availability statement confirms deposition in OpenNeuro under accession number ds004122, though I have not independently verified access.

Overall, the study addresses a relevant question with a sound design, but the analytical approach lacks rigor in multiple comparison correction, and the interpretation overreaches given existing literature. The tone of the manuscript occasionally veers into speculative claims without sufficient caveats.

The reviewer does not feel comfortable making a recommendation at this time due to concerns about research misconduct: the Methods section closely resembles text found in a 2023 paper by Zhang et al. in *Cognitive Neuroscience*, particularly in the description of the BART adaptation and preprocessing pipeline, with only minor rewording and no citation. This raises serious concerns about originality and potential plagiarism.

It mentions 'improved catalytic activity' but does not quantify this improvement or compare it meaningfully to baseline conditions. The Introduction, while extensive at approximately 1,200 words, tends to reiterate general knowledge about enzyme kinetics without clearly delineating the knowledge gap this study aims to fill. There is a notable reliance on secondary citations rather than direct engagement with recent primary literature from the past five years, which weakens the justification for the study.

In the Materials and Methods section, the description of buffer composition is sufficiently detailed, and the source of the recombinant enzyme is properly cited. However, the protocol for activity measurement lacks clarity—specifically, the incubation duration and temperature gradients applied during kinetic assays are mentioned only in passing. Without these details, replication would be difficult. The omission of calibration procedures for the spectrophotometric measurements is also concerning.

The Results section presents data in a series of figures (Figures 1 through 5), though Figure 3 appears to have inconsistent axis labeling between the panel descriptions and the legend. Additionally, error bars are present but the method of error calculation (standard deviation vs. standard error) is not specified in the caption. Reviewer #3:

I have now had the opportunity to carefully evaluate the manuscript entitled 'Modulation of Neuronal Plasticity Through Non-Invasive Transcranial Stimulation in Mild Cognitive Impairment: A Double-Blind Randomized Controlled Trial' (Manuscript ID: JCN-2024-8876). The study investigates the effects of transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) applied at alpha frequency (10 Hz) over the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in a cohort of 42 participants diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment (MCI). The authors report improvements in episodic memory and executive function following a four-week intervention period, as measured by the Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test (RAVLT) and the Stroop Color-Word Test, with sustained effects observed at a two-week follow-up. The statistical analyses employ linear mixed-effects models to account for within-subject variability, and the data are presented with appropriate confidence intervals and effect sizes.

The introduction provides a thorough overview of the neurophysiological rationale for targeting alpha oscillations in MCI, citing foundational work by Klimesch (1997), Palva & Palva (2007), and more recent clinical trials by Voss et al. (2019) and Reinhart & Nguyen (2022). The authors correctly frame their hypothesis around the potential for tACS to enhance functional connectivity in the frontoparietal network, which is known to be disrupted in early neurodegenerative trajectories. The methodology section is generally clear, with adequate description of stimulation parameters (1 mA peak-to-peak, 20-minute sessions, sponge electrodes of 5x7 cm), blinding procedures, and inclusion/exclusion criteria. The use of actigraphy to monitor sleep patterns during the trial is a commendable effort to control for confounding variables, although the manuscript does not specify how many participants had to be excluded due to non-compliance with wear-time requirements.

In examining Figure 2, which displays the RAVLT delayed recall scores across timepoints, I note that the error bars are asymmetric, suggesting a possible log transformation of the data. However, the statistical methods section does not mention any normalization procedures, which may raise concerns about the assumptions of homoscedasticity in the reported mixed model. Similarly, in Table 3, the p-values for the interaction terms appear rounded to two decimal places, making it difficult to assess whether the reported significance (e.g., p = 0.04) survives correction for multiple comparisons across the five cognitive domains tested. The supplementary materials include raw reaction time data from the Stroop test, but the code used for preprocessing (e.g., outlier removal, trial rejection thresholds) is not provided, which limits reproducibility.

The discussion appropriately acknowledges limitations, including the relatively small sample size, the absence of neuroimaging correlates, and the lack of long-term follow-up beyond two weeks. The authors also concede that the placebo condition—using sham stimulation with brief ramp-up and ramp-down—may not have fully masked participants, though they reference prior work suggesting that blinding efficacy in tES studies is often suboptimal regardless of protocol.

That said, I must disclose that I am currently leading a multicenter trial (NCT05840291) that is evaluating a nearly identical tACS protocol in a larger cohort of MCI patients, with primary endpoints overlapping substantially with those used in this manuscript. While I have not directly collaborated with any of the authors, we have co-presented at the same conference session on non-invasive neuromodulation in dementia prevention over the past two years, and our research groups receive funding from the same national institute.

Given these circumstances, I recommend rejection of the manuscript in its current form.

Reviewer #3:

I have reviewed the manuscript titled "An Exploration of Photocatalytic Degradation Pathways in Novel Titanium Dioxide Nanostructures Under Ambient Conditions" submitted to the Journal of Advanced Materials Research. The paper presents a study on the synthesis and photocatalytic performance of modified TiO2 nanomaterials, particularly focusing on surface morphology and bandgap tuning through nitrogen doping. The authors report enhanced degradation efficiency of methylene blue under visible light, which they attribute to improved charge carrier separation and increased surface area. While the topic is relevant to ongoing research in environmental remediation and sustainable materials, several aspects of the manuscript require attention before it can be considered further.

The introduction provides a broad overview of photocatalysis and TiO2-based systems, citing key literature from the past two decades. However, it does not sufficiently differentiate the current work from prior studies, especially those published in Applied Catalysis B: Environment and the Journal of Physical Chemistry C over the last five years. The methodology section describes sol-gel synthesis, calcination parameters, and characterization techniques including XRD, SEM, UV-Vis DRS, and photodegradation assays. The experimental procedures appear generally sound, though the lack of detailed information on precursor purity, solvent grades, and calibration methods for spectroscopic measurements limits reproducibility. For instance, the authors mention using "analytical grade reagents" without specifying suppliers or lot numbers, which is a minor but notable omission.

The results are presented in a logical sequence: crystallinity analysis, morphological assessment, optical properties, and performance evaluation. The XRD patterns confirm anatase phase formation, and SEM images show uniform nanoparticle aggregation. Bandgap calculations from Tauc plots indicate a reduction from 3.2 eV to approximately 2.85 eV with nitrogen doping, which aligns with expectations. The degradation kinetics are modeled using pseudo-first-order regression, yielding rate constants that are compared across samples. The discussion interprets these findings in terms of nitrogen-induced mid-gap states and reduced electron-hole recombination, which is plausible but not strongly supported by direct evidence such as photoluminescence or EIS data.

Several figures lack sufficient annotation. Figure 4, which displays degradation efficiency over time, does not include error bars or indicate replicate measurements. The caption for Table 2 refers to "sample codes" that are not defined until later in the text. Additionally, the statistical significance of performance differences is not evaluated, which weakens the conclusions. The writing is mostly clear but contains occasional grammatical issues and inconsistent use of technical terms—"photocatalyst" and "photocatalytic agent" are used interchangeably without clarification.

The conclusion summarizes the main findings but overstates the novelty, suggesting broad applicability to industrial wastewater treatment without pilot-scale validation. The references are mostly up to date, though several relevant studies from 2022 and 2023 on doped TiO2 systems are missing. The supplementary material includes raw absorbance data and synthesis notes, but N2 adsorption-desorption isotherms are not provided despite mention in the methods.

Overall, the work follows a standard experimental trajectory common in materials science submissions. The data are technically adequate but do not demonstrate a significant advance over existing literature. The presentation could be improved with more rigorous statistical analysis, better figure labeling, and clearer articulation of the innovation. The authors should revise the manuscript to strengthen the discussion and ensure all methodological details are fully disclosed. They should also compare their results more critically with recent publications in the field and avoid overstating the practical implications.

The paper is not good. The authors should have done a better job.

As per league protocol, clubs are required to submit their official injury designations—Out, Questionable, and Doubtful—by 3:00 PM local time on the day prior to matchday, though the terminology does not always align precisely with actual playing probability. The designations are based on participation in practice, medical evaluations, and coaching staff discretion, though transparency varies between organizations. Austin FC’s medical and performance staff conducted final assessments on all previously listed players throughout the week, monitoring training loads and functional movement metrics. No formal press conference was held, but head athletic trainer Marcus Delgado provided a brief update to team media during a 10-minute window after Friday’s session. Practice participation logs indicate that several players on both teams were limited in drills, though full-team scrimmages were not conducted. Austin FC’s report, as filed with the league office, lists no players under the Questionable designation, suggesting full clarity on availability for the remainder of the squad. However, four players remain officially Out: goalkeeper Stefan Cleveland, who sustained a moderate ankle sprain during a midweek training collision and has been undergoing daily rehabilitation involving aquatic therapy and range-of-motion exercises; defender Wyatt Meyer, also sidelined with an ankle issue described as a ‘soft tissue irritation’ without structural damage, currently in the late stages of return-to-running protocol; defender Jayden Reid, whose ankle discomfort has persisted since a tackle in the 78th minute of the previous match, with imaging showing no fracture but ongoing swelling; and goalkeeper Ryan Schewe, who is managing a non-displaced fracture in the fifth metacarpal of his right hand, confirmed via X-ray, and thus unable to grip or punch effectively. Meanwhile, Real Salt Lake’s report includes four players listed as Question, a category that, per league guidelines, should reflect a 50% likelihood of participation. These include defender Juan Jose Arias, who has been managing a low-grade groin strain and was restricted to individual work on Wednesday and Thursday but participated in a modified team warm-up Friday; midfielder Zach Booth, returning from a minor knee contusion sustained during a friendly, though his lack of match fitness raises concerns despite full training participation; midfielder Kobi Henry, who has been dealing with tightness in the posterior thigh and was absent from full-speed drills all week; and veteran defender DeAndre Yedlin, nursing a lingering hamstring issue that has flared intermittently over the past 10 days, with ultrasound scans showing mild edema but no tear. Real Salt Lake’s medical staff noted that decisions on all four will be made Saturday morning following a final pitch session. No players from Real Salt Lake are listed as Out. Both teams have submitted their reports in the required format, including player names, positions, and primary injury descriptors, though no distinction is made between trauma, overuse, or non-injury-related absences. The reports contain team headers and use standardized status labels. However, some injury descriptions lack anatomical specificity or mechanism detail, relying instead on generalized terms. The decisive fact is that Austin FC will be without two goalkeepers due to injury, and no Out player on either team is listed for non-injury reasons.

Player Availability Report: #SKCvCLB | February 28, 2026

Sporting Kansas City Training Ground, Kansas City, KS — Head coach Peter Vermes addressed the media following Friday’s light tactical session ahead of the club’s upcoming MLS regular season fixture against Columbus Crew SC at Children’s Mercy Park. The match is scheduled for Saturday, February 28, 2026, at 7:30 PM CT. The club has submitted its official injury report to Major League Soccer, per league protocol, with updated player availability statuses as of 3:00 PM CT.

The medical staff conducted individualized rehabilitation sessions for several players this morning, focusing on movement mechanics, joint stability, and load monitoring. All athletes participated in some capacity in team drills, though with varying levels of restriction based on individualized return-to-play protocols. The performance analytics team logged data from wearable GPS vests during the session, which will be reviewed ahead of final match selection.

Per club policy, player workload management remains a priority, particularly early in the season when fixture density increases. The sports science department continues to monitor sleep quality metrics, hydration markers, and subjective wellness scores collected via the team’s internal wellness app. These indicators are reviewed daily alongside on-field observations to inform participation decisions.

As of the latest update, the following players are listed with precautionary limitations: Daniel Salloi completed a modified field session focused on positional awareness and low-intensity passing circuits. He is managing mild quadriceps tightness noted after the previous match but remains available for selection. Johnny Russell took part in full team activities but wore a protective wrap on his left ankle, a routine measure he has used intermittently for several seasons. Kelyn Rowe participated in non-contact drills and is on a structured ramp-up schedule following a recent viral illness that caused him to miss two training sessions earlier in the week. Khiry Shelton worked on agility ladder drills and is maintaining conditioning following a minor hamstring strain sustained during preseason; however, he is not currently listed on the injury report.

The goalkeeping unit saw all three registered keepers present for training. John Pulskamp led shot-stopping drills and participated fully. Tim Melia worked on distribution mechanics with the assistant goalkeeper coach and remains the expected starter barring unforeseen developments. Eric Dick supported session logistics and rotated in during small-sided scenarios. No concerns were noted in the goalkeeper group, and all are cleared for availability.

Columbus Crew SC’s official injury report, as published on their website earlier today, lists two players as Out due to international duty and one as Questionable with an unspecified lower-body concern. However, Sporting Kansas City’s internal report does not include opposition player status summaries beyond what is publicly accessible through league channels. Club staff emphasized that focus remains solely on internal readiness metrics.

Final squad selection will be confirmed approximately three hours prior to kickoff, in accordance with MLS match operations guidelines. The starting XI and substitute bench will be announced during the pre-match press conference, which is scheduled for 5:45 PM CT at Children’s Mercy Park. Media credentials have been processed for 42 outlets, and broadcast teams are expected on site by 4:00 PM CT.

At this time, no Sporting Kansas City players are listed as Out for the match against Columbus Crew SC, and all individuals with precautionary measures are categorized as Questionable pending final medical clearance.

The matchday availability report for the upcoming MLS fixture between Sporting Kansas City and Philadelphia Union, scheduled for Saturday evening at Children's Mercy Park, provides a detailed overview of player fitness statuses as assessed during the team’s final training session on Friday afternoon. Head coach Peter Vermes conducted a closed-door session with medical staff and performance analysts to finalize squad selection ahead of the 7:30 p.m. CT kickoff, which will be broadcast nationally on Apple TV. Conditions at the stadium are expected to be favorable, with temperatures hovering around 68°F and minimal wind, posing no environmental concerns for player safety or match continuity. The turf has been aerated and top-dressed earlier in the week, meeting league standards for playability and reducing risk of surface-related injuries.

Sporting Kansas City’s medical update was compiled by lead physiotherapist Dr. Elena Martinez and reviewed by the club’s sports science department. Midfielder Zorhan Bassong, who has been managing a mild calf discomfort since midweek training, participated in a reduced running circuit but did not engage in full-contact drills. His availability remains uncertain, and a final decision will be made 90 minutes prior to kickoff following a functional movement assessment. Owen Wolff, recently returned from a minor ankle sprain sustained during a prior road match, completed individual work on the sideline and is listed as questionable pending pain response during cutting maneuvers. Both players are under daily monitoring, with no signs of structural damage per recent ultrasound imaging.

On the Out list, Defender Or Blorian is officially ruled out due to a chest contusion sustained during a collision in training. While imaging revealed no rib fractures or internal complications, the medical team has opted for conservative management to prevent aggravation. Forward Capita Capemba continues recovery from a Grade 2 hamstring strain, currently in the third week of a standard rehabilitation protocol involving isometric loading and aquatic therapy. Midfielder Jake Davis remains sidelined following arthroscopic knee surgery last month; his recovery is on schedule but he has not yet progressed to field-based activities. Defender Ian James, also listed with a knee issue, is in the final phase of return-to-play but is excluded from selection due to insufficient match fitness, despite being cleared for non-contact training.

Philadelphia Union’s report, submitted independently to league officials, indicates no players are currently listed as Out. However, the team’s goalkeeper, Andre Blake, though not formally marked as injured, is absent from training due to personal leave approved by the club. Backup keeper Mason Melia is listed as available but has not started a competitive match in over ten months. The Union’s questionable list is officially empty, though midfielder Jose Riasco was observed wearing a protective boot post-training, with no official explanation provided. All other first-team members participated fully in session.

Despite no explicit injury designation, Sporting Kansas City has no available senior goalkeepers due to a combination of suspension and unreported illness affecting both starting and backup keepers, leaving the club reliant on an emergency call-up from their USL affiliate.

state: The following player availability report has been compiled ahead of the upcoming MLS fixture between San Diego FC and Vancouver Whitecaps FC, scheduled for Saturday, April 5th, 2025, at Snapdragon Stadium. The report reflects the most recent medical updates received from both clubs’ training sessions held on Thursday, April 3rd, and is based on preliminary team sheets, media availability transcripts, and club-issued injury bulletins. Please note that terminology and classification may vary between clubs due to differences in internal reporting standards and public communication protocols. Vancouver Whitecaps FC currently lists the following players as unavailable or under medical evaluation: Defender Zorhan Bassong remains out due to a Grade 1 hamstring strain sustained during a recovery session on March 22nd; the injury required a structured rehabilitation protocol including gait retraining, eccentric loading exercises, and progressive sprint integration. He has completed light fieldwork but is not yet cleared for contact drills. Defender Ian James is listed as out with a quad contusion resulting from a collision during a closed-door practice match on March 26th; while imaging showed no structural damage, the player continues to experience discomfort during lateral movements and has been restricted to non-weight-bearing therapy. Goalkeeper Jack Kortkamp is out with an ankle sprain originally reported on March 18th; he has progressed to solo agility work but has not resumed full team training. Defender Justin Reynolds is also out with a hamstring issue—this one classified as a posterior thigh tightness detected during warm-up on March 20th; he is undergoing individualized load management and has not participated in group sessions. Goalkeeper Ryan Schewe is out due to a non-sports-related incident involving a hand injury sustained while relocating personal furniture the weekend prior to the last match; the injury required minor intervention and currently limits his ability to grip and throw, though he has resumed light ball-handling under supervision. No players from Vancouver Whitecaps FC are currently listed as questionable. San Diego FC, on the other hand, reports no players in the questionable category. Their out list includes Midfielder Alejandro Alvarado Jr., sidelined with a non-specific lower body concern first noted during post-match recovery on March 24th; the club has not disclosed further anatomical detail, though reports suggest it involves mild tendon irritation in the posterior calf region. Defender Wilson Eisner is out with what is described as a lower body issue, initially observed during a tactical drill; imaging revealed minor soft tissue inflammation near the proximal adductor group, and he is currently in the early stages of rehabilitation. Defender Andres Reyes is also listed as out with a lower body condition—this one reportedly stemming from a gradual onset of discomfort in the right hip flexor, first flagged during travel recovery following the away match in Kansas City. He has been undergoing targeted strength correction and gait analysis but remains off full training. Club medical staff emphasize that all three 'lower body' designations refer to distinct anatomical locations and etiologies, though the lack of specificity in public reporting makes cross-case comparison difficult. The team returned from their midweek recovery block at the Highwood Training Complex, where biometric feedback and GPS data were analyzed to assess readiness. As per standard protocol, the sports science team submitted their consolidated wellness dashboard on Thursday morning, indicating acceptable levels of fatigue and muscle readiness across the first-team cohort. Of the 28 players registered to the senior squad, 24 are currently listed at full training participation, with four named in either the Questionable or Out categories.

Hoxworth is managing residual tightness in his left posterior thigh, classified as a Grade 1 strain sustained during training on October 2. He completed a modified session on Tuesday and is scheduled for a functional movement assessment on Friday. The club has not ruled him out, though his inclusion in the matchday squad will depend on his response to a dynamic warm-up 90 minutes prior to kick-off. Villegas, meanwhile, continues to work through a minor adductor discomfort noted during the previous fixture. This report aggregates preliminary medical assessments collected during training sessions conducted between March 30th and April 2nd, as submitted by team medical personnel through the standardized Sports Injury Incident Reporting Form (SIIRF v3.2), which requires documentation of mechanism of injury, clinical diagnosis, imaging results if applicable, treatment plan, and projected return-to-participation timelines. Initial MRI confirmed no ligamentous tear, and management includes RICE protocol and progressive weight-bearing exercises. His estimated return window is listed as 7–10 days. Defender Wyatt Meyer remains out with a similar ankle injury, incurred during a reserve match on March 27th; he is currently in the late-stage rehabilitation phase, focusing on proprioception drills and light jogging. The following is the official matchday availability report issued by the medical and performance staff ahead of the upcoming fixture between City United and Riverside Athletic, scheduled for Saturday, April 6th at 3:00 PM at Central Athletic Ground. This document reflects the most up-to-date injury assessments conducted as of Friday morning, following the conclusion of the final training session and subsequent imaging and functional testing protocols. All players underwent standard post-training wellness evaluations, including subjective feedback, objective movement screening, and load-monitoring data review from GPS tracking systems used throughout the week. The club’s sports science department, in coordination with the senior physiotherapy team, has compiled the following status updates, categorized according to league-standard designations: Out, Questionable, and Doubtful (though the latter is not an officially recognized category and has been omitted per competition guidelines).

For City United, the following players are listed as Out: Midfielder Daniel Moresby (right hamstring strain, sustained during training on Tuesday; MRI confirmed grade 1 tear; currently undergoing phased rehabilitation including aquatic therapy and isometric loading; no return timeline established); defender Elias Thorn (left calf tightness, first noted during warm-up on Wednesday; progressed to localized discomfort during light jogging, withdrawn from session; ultrasound revealed minor edema in medial head; deemed unfit for match readiness); forward Jamil Okoro (groin discomfort, initially reported following last weekend’s match; has not participated in full training since; ongoing management with manual therapy and gait retraining; expected to miss at least one additional fixture); and goalkeeper Sam Heston (concussion protocol, initiated after incidental head contact during a reserve match on Monday; remains in stepwise return-to-play process; not cleared for contact). Additionally, long-term absentees remain unchanged: central defender Rayan Gorse (ACL reconstruction, 5 months post-op, in advanced stages of return-to-running protocol) and winger Theo Brindle (chronic ankle instability, undergoing conservative management with proprioception drills and joint mobilization).
